extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural designers, students of architecture, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive design and critical principles for honest, durable, and morally sound architecture — focusing on truthful use of materials, ornament, mouldings, and composition. Emphasises hand-work, appropriate material use, and avoidance of deceptive display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty of ornament / avoidance of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments or finishes that pretend to a worth they do not possess are an imposition, a vulgarity, an impertinence, and a sin; better to leave walls bare than to rough-cast them with falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists that using any decorative device which pretends to be what it is not (e.g., falsely imitating more costly material or workmanship) is unacceptable. Examples and injunctions: do not wear false jewels; do not rough-cast walls to look like carved stone; 'Down with it to the ground, grind it to powder' rather than keep false ornament. Integrity is placed above ornament: 'Nobody wants ornaments in this world, but everybody wants integrity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of visible human hand-work
rubrics_metrics.description: The worth and delight of ornament largely arise from the consciousness that it is the work of human thought, trials, and craftsmanship — the record of the human hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works wrought by human hand (even in cheaper materials) can be more precious than mechanically-produced luxury (e.g., a hand-wrought piece of terra cotta or plaster may be worth more than Carrara stone cut by machinery). The presence of the hand imparts intrinsic moral and aesthetic value, detectable by a practised eye; beware of machine work that attempts to masquerade as hand-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use materials according to their nature and expected production
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials that are known to be moulded or cast (brick, tile, porcelain, clay, iron, bronze) may legitimately be shaped and ornamented accordingly; materials naturally supposed to be carved (stone) must not be represented as cast or machine-carved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted: elaborate cast brick mouldings (Palazzo Pepoli, Vercelli); tile and porcelain ornament (French domestic architecture, Tuscan bas-reliefs by the Robbia family). Prohibited: artificial stone cast into shape, stucco ornament which might be mistaken for carved stone (e.g., stucco mouldings in the cortile of the Palazzo Vecchio) and machine-carved stone that pretends to be hand-carved. The rule: do not make a material appear to have been produced by a method it was not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject cheap mechanical substitutes (cast iron and similar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant use of cast iron ornaments and other cheap substitutes has actively degraded the natural feeling for beauty; they are cold, clumsy, vulgar, and incapable of fine line or shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast medieval wrought or hammered iron (simple and effective) with modern cast iron work (cold and paltry). While cast iron is distinguishable from wrought work and thus not directly false, its pervasiveness corrupts taste and undermines the progress of the arts when employed where it may claim undeserved credit or associate with dignified work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mass as the primary element rather than mere decorative line
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute line for mass as the chief element of decoration; the shift from mass to the line (as seen in tracery) marked a profound and ultimately detrimental change in the spirit of Gothic architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical account: traceries began by emphasizing openings (light) and mass; when stone-work became slender lines and the architect's eye turned to those lines, the intervening spaces were discarded and decoration became line-dominated. This substitution led to a brief pause of excellence but then to decline as attention moved away from the nobler character of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express truthful material properties (avoid implying ductility or penetrability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture must express the true qualities of its materials (stiffness, weight, limits of strength); it is false to represent stone or masonry as if they were ductile, elastic, or penetrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns traceries and mouldings drawn to look like woven or flexible threads (as if stone were silken cord) or as if one moulding penetrates another. Such representations 'sacrifice the expression of the qualities of the material' and constitute a deliberate treachery. Use analogies (e.g., tree branches vs stone ribs) carefully — similarity in appearance does not justify misrepresenting structural behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive intersectional mouldings and fictive construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not design mouldings so that they appear to pass through or be penetrated by one another, or to imply a construction that is not actually present; intersections should be managed honestly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, great periods melted mouldings into each other by contact, sharing sections; later builders made mouldings preserve independent existence and manufactured clever intersectional lines to display skill. Examples: Lisieux door shafts, Palazzo Foscari, Rouen. Such intersectional trickery prioritizes dexterity over truth and 'crushed the art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Eschew display of mere dexterity or ingenious device
rubrics_metrics.description: Sternly disdain all display of technical dexterity and ingenious trickery; instead concentrate imaginative energy on the arrangement of masses and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises putting 'the whole force of our fancy into the arrangement of masses and forms,' caring not for minute technical display (as a great painter cares not which way his pencil strikes). Excessive attention to clever stone-cutting or 'architectural sleight of hand' catches the fancy of the uninventive and leads to decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against subtle deceptions that appeal to fancy and sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be watchful of subtle forms of deception that affect impression and idea (not physically false), for though some may be nobly used, most are legerdemain that lower the style and may be widely adopted by uninventive practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the arborescent look of lofty Gothic aisles may be noble, but many such effects are trickery or 'legerdemain' that will lower any style where they prevail. Such subtleties are hard to legislate against and must be countered by a manly and unaffected spirit and critical vigilance rather than by fixed rules alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity as the supreme imperative above ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrity (truth, honesty of construction and material) is a more imperative law than ornament; ornament is inessential and must never be allowed to be fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text elevates integrity over adornment: ornament is extravagant and inessential; if it is fallacious it is utterly base. Therefore ornament must never deceive or pretend; when in doubt, favor integrity even at the cost of simplicity or absence of ornament.
